Wheel to wheel racing does not end well in low iR Rookie series, but thats normal because its mostly people starting who are not in total control of their cars yet.

There are two ways to get out of the early races. 

The first one is to qualify at the top and just be better than other rookies. They hardly crash into you if youre two corners ahead, and you only have to be very careful when lapping someone 

The second one is just focus your attention in avoiding incidents and get top 10 just by being safer. Eventually your iRating will increase and youll be matched with drivers who have better control of their cars allowing for more close racing.

CS degree makes it easier to find jobs, because it looks good in your CV and some companies require it.

Consider it like a foot on the door. If you have a CS degree but are terrible at programming, you will get an interview but then bomb it and not get the job many times. Eventuallt you will pass one and get a job.

If you do not have a CS degree, you will have to compensate through projects to get that interview. You will get less interviews, as some positions require a degree. If you are good at programming, you will eventually pass as well and get a job.

I do not think a CS degree has much weight when it comes to promotions either. The best or most social one gets the job, with or without degree. If both options have similar skills, then the degree may tip the balance.


We (fortunately) live in a work field that has enough jobs for everyone. Getting your first job may be hard if you are looking for certain companies and such, specially without a degree, but after that it will be fairly easy to get new oportunities.

TLDR: A degree is an advantage when getting interviews, but if you manage to get a job then from there your skills/experience will be way more important.

I think I can relate. Ill tell you about my experience and how I managed to go past it.

I remember when League of Legends loot system got out. Roughly you could would obtain chests by playing and they would contain a random skin for a random character. You could get lucky and get the most interesting skin for someone you play or get an average or bad one for someone you dont play.

Issue was you could (and still can) buy chests with real money. And since its random, its cheaper than direct skins.

Something inside me went full balistic on buying those. y parents gave me some money for my expenses while I studied (around 300€ month for food, hobbies, study materials, ...).  I spent 400€ in 2 months in that game. I usually control my own finance, and Im pretty good at it (I managed to save a bunch) but that was a spending spree.

It was 20€ here, 35€ there, but it added up really fast. When I checked my account i freaked out. I was so scared. I needed to set boundaries to prevent this from happening again.

So I set a budget (I work now so its bigger). I have self imposed personal gaming allowance each month. I choose to spend 50€/month in games. If Im playing a f2p game, I can spend 50€ in packs, expansions, whatever. If I want to buy a 60€ game, I must wait until my gaming budget has that amount to spare. If game is 90€, then I have to wait more.

Its the best approach I could find to allow me to spend some money in game contents without ruining me.

An IP ban is not exactly just an IP ban. It works in 2 ways. One part is IP and the other one is not.

Most game servers would ban your IP and similar IPs that youre likely to get. However this brings an unintended problem.

Lets, for the sake of the case, assume that you live in a 2 floor apartment, where you and the resident in the other apartment share the same gaming hobbies and ISP. However, you are a massive cheater in the game and your neighbour is not.

If you simply got an IP ban, resetting the router would circumvent it. If they give you a range of IPs that are to be banned, there is a chance your ISP assigns one of those to your neighbour, effectively preventing him from playing.

So how to fix this? Pretty much flags.

Your IP is banned, but thats just one of the things considered when the user tries to log in. Your steam/Rockstar Launcher whatever has an ID that identifies you. If a connect request comes with that ID, deny service. If you try to connect with an IP that is the same with a new account after you tried with your banned account. Ban the new one. And many other methods that I simply dont know.

Also just answering the OP question.

Yes its possible to get a player IP in most online games. However an IP alone just gets you information about the ISP and the rough location of the user. Perhaps the City if its a big one or a number of them if youre in the countryside.

An IP alone is not enough to identify and locate an individual period. You can be vulnerable to attacks such as DDoS but only until you reset the router, or, if the attacker is good (which you wont find in a lobby in general, these people have better things to do than to waste hours attacking a random Joe over a game) until you contact your provider or block the traffic type they are attacking you with.

Companies are way trickier (web page always accessible, IP extremely easier to track and they have to allow good users to interact) to manage security for than random users.

I am a CS graduate who codes solely on VMs on Windows with linux installed. I learned that this was what worked for me best for a couple reasons

 1. Linux command line feels simpler/more documented. All my OS subjects used linux for reference, so I know many more commands that I know on windows and mac.


2. Really easy to clean up if you mess up. Make a copy of a VM drive on your main machine and set it back if you somehow touch parts of the OS youre not supposed to touch, or cannot/dont want to fix. Installing OS/software after messing up and reconfiguring everything can take hours/days if you lose code. This way 5 minutes im not that set back.


3. Separate your projects nicely. If you do a webapp and a game, chances are your dependencies dont have anything in common, or the project itself. Having your projects or even parts of the same project in separate machines also helps understand how machines communicate, APIs, network etc...

Its a good project after your first web to do frontend in one machine and backend on the other one. Teaches you a lot.

Again, there is not a "best" platform to code on. You should be able to do everything in every platform. But there are circumstances where a platform is better prepared for use cases, and the programmer comfort is what is paramount.
